analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to disclose wage ranges in job postings and to current employees.
analysis.headline: The Salary Transparency Act was introduced with no cosponsors and never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Fair Labor Standards Act to make it unlawful for an employer to post a job opening without a wage or salary range, to withhold a range from applicants, or to withhold from employees the range for their own position upon hire and annually thereafter [S3]. It would also ban retaliation against workers who exercise these rights [S3]. Violations would carry civil penalties up to $10,000 and private lawsuits with damages between $1,000 and $10,000 or actual damages, plus attorneys' fees [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Job applicants and current employees, who would learn what a job actually pays before applying, negotiating, or accepting it. The bill text defines the required disclosure to include salary, other compensation reasonably expected, applicable pay scales, and ranges for people already holding equivalent positions [S3]. Pay transparency has been associated in state and city studies with narrower pay gaps, which matters most for women and workers of color who are likeliest to be offered less than peers for the same work.

how_it_helps.text: Employers must post the wage or wage range — including salary, other compensation, and the range for equivalent current positions — in any public or internal job posting [S3].
Applicants must be told the range before any compensation discussion and on request; employees must be told the range for their own position at hire and at least annually, and on request [S3].
The bill makes it unlawful to refuse to interview, hire, promote, or employ someone, or otherwise retaliate, for exercising these rights [S3].

Enforcement is real money: $5,000 civil penalty for a first violation rising to $10,000, plus statutory damages of $1,000–$10,000 or actual damages (whichever is greater) and attorneys' fees, enforceable by employees individually and in group actions [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers — particularly those that currently negotiate pay secretly and benefit from information asymmetry — would bear compliance costs, disclosure of internal pay structures, penalty exposure, and the risk of group lawsuits. They would also lose a negotiating tool: a job seeker who knows the budgeted range cannot be anchored to a lower offer.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers that benefit from pay secrecy

drawbacks.text: Disclosure requirements impose administrative work on employers of every size, and penalties of $5,000–$10,000 per violation with group-litigation exposure could invite suits over good-faith range-setting, which the bill leaves to employer judgment [S3].

Some economists argue posted ranges compress flexibility: firms posting ranges may set them wide or shift compensation into unlisted forms, and pay transparency alone does not force raises — it gives workers information, not bargaining power.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — workers knowing the pay before they apply or negotiate — is concrete and cheap to deliver; comparable state and city laws have operated without disrupting hiring. The compliance and litigation costs are real but modest relative to the information gain for tens of millions of job seekers. The bill's main weakness is not design but design detail: it relies on employers' good faith in setting ranges and provides no guidance on range width. On balance it is a straightforward worker-information bill.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Delegate Eleanor Holmes Norton introduced the Salary Transparency Act on February 25, 2022, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the same day [S1][S5].
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no report — and the bill never reached the House floor; the Congress ended January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that prefer not to disclose pay ranges are better off: the bill died in committee without a single cosponsor, so no federal transparency requirement took effect. Workers' option to know a job's pay range before applying or negotiating remains governed by a patchwork of state and local laws instead.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers that keep pay ranges secret

for.name: Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; referred it to committee by the rules of the House.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it died in committee at the end of the Congress.

against.name: 0 of 434 House members (other than the sponsor)
against.what_they_did: None signed on as cosponsors, leaving the bill with no demonstrated support beyond its sponsor.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no other member cosponsored, so the partisan shape of the bill's support was never measured; the only recorded positions are its Democratic sponsor and the committee's inaction.

industries.note: The bill would force employers to publish wage ranges in postings, disclose ranges to employees annually, and expose them to penalties and group lawsuits for violations [S3]. Its cost to them is the loss of pay secrecy, a tool that lets employers set pay one worker at a time.
Applicants and employees would gain the right to know the pay range for any job they pursue or hold, with damages and attorneys' fees as enforcement teeth [S3].
